problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{3}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{y}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$

feedback.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ can be used to transform the equation 

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & ={z}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{z}^{-1} \\ -x{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{z}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}+\frac{1}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-\frac{1}{x}.$
